catalog_quote: Chamorro is a language with stress. Each word has one syllable that bears primary stress (i.e. is louder or more prominent than the other syllables in the word). This syllable is generally the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable of the word. Primary stress is determined differently for roots (unaffixed words) than for affixed words. A substantial number of roots, most of them borrowed from Spanish, exceptionally have primary stress on the last syllable. ... /aˈsut/ ... A substantial number of roots exceptionally have primary stress on the antepenultimate (third-from-last) syllable. ... /ˈdeddigu/ ... /aˈpigigiʔ/ ... /ˈkunanaf/ ... All other roots have primary stress on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable. ... /ˈsajna/ ... /iˈlotis/ ... /kaˈdidak/ ... In affixed words, primary stress is determined by whether the affix is a suffix, an inherently stressed prefix, or some other morpheme…
sweep_summary: Two title hits, both by known Chamorro specialists. (1) Chung 2003 (LI 34) was downloaded from the author's UCSC page (Semantic Scholar green-OA link; saved with text). It is a syntax/prosody paper on weak-pronoun clitics; its single word-stress statement (p. 579-580: primary stress 'calculated from the right', falling on the penult of the prosodic word) confirms the catalog's penultimate coding but supplies nothing on exceptions. (2) Crosswhite 1998 (Phonology 15) is paywalled at Cambridge (Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar closed, no ROA copy); the abstract says it analyzes Saipanese Chamorro stress shifts under affixation in correspondence theory - a theoretical treatment that would refine the affixation facts but is unlikely to beat Chung 2020 as the deciding statement (priority medium). Note on the deciding source itself: re-reading Chung 2020 sec. 29.4.1 (pp. 660-663; excerpt saved) shows the catalog quote is truncated after the final-stress loans; the section continues 'A substantial number of roots exceptionally have primary stress on the antepenultimate (third-from-last) syllable' (e.g. /ˈdeddigu/, /ˈkunanaf/), stressed prefixes (a-, acha-, mi-, sen, gof, gai, tai..) take primary stress, and suffixes re-place stress on the penult of the suffixed word - i.e. the deciding source states substantial lexical exceptions in both directions, which the 'fixed-strict' register (exceptions falsify) should weigh; the record already carries lexical_stress='disputed'. lookups used Crossref, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Cambridge Core, ROA index and direct downloads.

sources.citation: Chung, Sandra. 2003. The Syntax and Prosody of Weak Pronouns in Chamorro. Linguistic Inquiry 34(4): 547-599.
sources.quote: Prosodic words in Chamorro are distinguished by the fact that they bear primary stress, which is calculated from the right. Among the many Chamorro processes sensitive to primary stress is the reduplication that realizes progressive aspect. When a predicate XP in Chamorro is inflected for progressive aspect, the inflection is realized on the leftmost prosodic word instantiating the XP, via reduplication of its primarily stressed CV (i.e., the onset and nucleus of the primarily stressed syllable, but not the coda). [p. 580:] (Had the combination of adjective and noun formed a single prosodic word, that word's primary stress would have fallen on the initial syllable of patgun 'child'; compare (58a).)
sources.locator: p. 579 (section 6.1, paragraph before ex. (57)); p. 580 (parenthetical after ex. (59))
sources.note: The paper is about the syntax and prosodic phrasing of weak (clitic) pronouns, not a description of word stress. Its only word-stress statement is that each prosodic word bears one primary stress 'calculated from the right'; the p. 580 example (stress would fall on the initial = penultimate syllable of a hypothetical adjective+noun prosodic word, patgun being disyllabic) shows the right-edge computation is penultimate. Weak pronouns are 'prosodically deficient enclitics: unstressed forms, mostly monosyllables' (p. 548). No exceptions or lexical-stress discussion.

sources.quote: In Chamorro, stressed syllables must be heavy; for open syllables, this is usually achieved by lengthening the vowel (e.g. /finu-ña/→[fi.ˈnu:.ña] ‘smoother’). Suffixation shifts stress rightwards and typically causes the stressed vowel of the stem to lengthen.

tone.quote: 抑揚。一語中の音の抑揚、卽ちアクセントについては劃然たる規則がないから、一つ一つの語について習得するの外はないが、大體に於て次の如くいひ得る。邦語と同樣に餘り目立つた抑揚はない。接合及熟合語に在つては主語にアクセントを置く。多くの場合接頭語を冠して居るから、其次にアクセントがあると思へば大差はない。
tone.locator: pp. 14-15, sec. 二 文字及發音 [2. Script and pronunciation], closing paragraph '抑揚'
tone.translation: Pitch modulation. As for the rise and fall of sounds within a word, that is, accent, there is no clear-cut rule, so there is nothing for it but to learn it word by word; but broadly one can say the following. As in Japanese, there is no very conspicuous pitch modulation. In joined and compound words the accent is placed on the main word. Since in most cases a prefix is attached, one will not be far wrong in assuming that the accent comes right after it.
